abstract: Brynjolfsson, Mitchell, and Rock develop the Suitability for Machine Learning (SML) rubric, a systematic framework for evaluating which occupational tasks are most amenable to automation by machine learning. Applied to 18,156 tasks in the O*NET occupational database, the rubric assesses each task against 21 criteria that determine ML suitability, including whether the task involves well-defined inputs and outputs, whether large training datasets exist, and whether the task requires physical dexterity or social perception. The central finding is that ML affects different occupations than earlier waves of automation — disrupting cognitive and analytical tasks rather than purely physical or routine manual ones. Most occupations contain a mix of SML-high and SML-low tasks, meaning few jobs are fully automatable by ML but many will be substantially restructured as high-SML tasks are automated while low-SML tasks remain human-performed. The authors emphasize that realizing ML's potential usually requires redesigning job task content, not simply dropping ML into existing workflows. This paper established one of the foundational frameworks for task-level automation analysis that subsequent research (including GPT-era exposure studies) has built upon.
keyFindings: ML affects different occupations than earlier automation waves, targeting cognitive and analytical tasks rather than physical or routine manual ones
Most occupations contain a mix of ML-suitable and ML-unsuitable tasks — few jobs are fully automatable but many will be restructured
Applied the SML rubric to 18,156 individual tasks across O*NET's occupational database
Realizing ML potential usually requires redesigning job task content, not simply deploying technology into existing workflows
Established a foundational framework for task-level automation analysis that subsequent research has built upon
methodology: Development and application of a 21-criteria Suitability for Machine Learning (SML) rubric to 18,156 tasks in the O*NET occupational database. Each task scored on criteria including input/output structure, training data availability, physical requirements, and social perception needs. Published in AEA Papers & Proceedings (2018). Cross-sectional task-level analysis.
qualifiers: Published in 2018, predating the generative AI era — the SML rubric was designed for traditional ML (supervised learning, classification, prediction) and may not fully capture the broader task range amenable to large language models and multimodal AI. Task-level analysis does not account for general equilibrium effects (new task creation, demand shifts). O*NET task descriptions may not match actual workplace task performance. The rubric assesses technical feasibility, not economic viability or adoption likelihood. Implementation barriers (regulatory, organizational, worker acceptance) are not modeled.
